source.title: Gaussian Universality of Linear Classifiers with Random Labels in High-Dimension
source.authors: Federica Gerace; Florent Krzakala; Bruno Loureiro; Ludovic Stephan; Lenka Zdeborov'a

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; no file problem noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains generalized linear classifiers on random labels and reports training loss, but it does not measure held-out error or any other behavior named by the claim versions. Its results therefore do not test those versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training loss on random-label tasks, including zero loss in an underdetermined ridgeless square-loss regime and empirical agreement between real-data training curves and Gaussian theory. These results concern training fit only; they do not measure natural-label test error or the training–test gap.
record.test_reason: The study measures random-label training loss and its agreement with Gaussian predictions. It reports no natural-label held-out performance, random-label held-out performance, or other outcome required by V1–V8. Random-label interpolation alone does not test V1's coexistence claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors establish Gaussian universality of random-label training loss under stated conditions and find close empirical agreement on several real datasets. Their conclusion also extends to models in the lazy regime through fixed-feature representations; non-convex losses, broader multilayer settings and non-random labels remain future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies convex empirical-risk minimization for generalized linear classifiers and fixed-feature models on random labels, rather than standard gradient training of networks on natural labels with held-out evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that agreement depends on conditions including regularization, homogeneity of mixture covariances, and preprocessing; raw datasets show small deviations, while a constructed heterogeneous Gaussian mixture shows deviations from strict universality.

fits_no_version.finding: Ridgeless square-loss classifiers have asymptotic random-label training loss equal to one-half times max(0, 1 − 1/α), under the stated assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-dimensional linear classifiers interpolate random labels in the underdetermined full-rank regime, with a universal minimum square-loss curve for Gaussian mixtures.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-label training-loss curves for fixed-feature real datasets closely match Gaussian predictions; raw datasets show small deviations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gaussian models approximate random-label training loss for several high-dimensional real datasets, with agreement depending on preprocessing and regularization.

record.problems: The reported experiments measure training loss, not generalization to held-out examples. The real-data experiments use fixed feature transforms and do not test end-to-end multilayer network training. Error bars are reported as not visible at the plot scale; the paper notes small deviations for raw data and for a constructed heterogeneous mixture.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Figures 1–5 contain plotted curves, but the text provides the relevant aggregate descriptions; precise per-curve values were not reconstructed from figures.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label memorization and above-chance natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe, including chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Held-out error as network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Held-out performance of convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error across training-set sizes, dropout strengths and augmentation settings.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The corrected states indicate that these measures cannot determine V1–V8, rather than disputing the reported training-loss findings. The heterogeneous-mixture counterexample in Figure 3 qualifies Gaussian universality, not any supplied claim version.

versions.untested_parts: Natural-label held-out accuracy, random-label held-out accuracy, and their comparison under the same architectures and recipes.
Network width sweeps and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and image test error.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparisons and held-out performance.
Batch-size comparisons and held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: Perceptron (generalized linear classifier)
rows.size_stated: Input dimension p; proportional high-dimensional limit with n/p → α
rows.operation_detail: Minimized empirical risk with random labels; ridgeless limit of ridge regression with square loss.

conditions.value: Gaussian mixture, arbitrary means, covariances, and proportions

rows.note: The stated expression is zero for α ≤ 1 and positive for α > 1. This is training loss, not held-out performance.
rows.check: The formula correctly describes random-label training loss, but cannot establish any version's generalization effect. The stated universality requires the paper's high-dimensional regularity and rank assumptions; Appendix A notes that rank replaces dimension for rank-deficient designs.

rows.subject: Generalized linear classifiers on real datasets with fixed feature maps
rows.operation_detail: Trained on random labels while varying n/p; compared training-loss curves with Gaussian theory.

conditions.value: MNIST with Gaussian random features and erf; fashion-MNIST with wavelet scattering; grayscale CIFAR-10 with Gaussian random features and ReLU
finite and vanishing values, depending on figure

rows.measure: Training loss as a function of n/p
rows.baseline: Gaussian theory with matching covariance at finite regularization; unit-covariance Gaussian theory at vanishing regularization
rows.value: Authors state that the real-data training curves agree with the corresponding Gaussian theory; Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 show the curves.
rows.uncertainty: Fig. 2 simulations averaged over 10 samples; error bars not visible at plot scale.
rows.locator: Summary of main results; Section IV; Figures 1–2
rows.note: Aggregate description across the listed datasets and feature maps; the paper says the losses are indistinguishable in the vanishing-regularization plots and that the finite-regularization theory fits the simulations. No held-out error is reported.
rows.check: Agreement with Gaussian training-loss predictions is reported, but does not measure any claim version. This aggregate combines datasets, losses and regularization settings: Figure 1 shows square and hinge losses at vanishing regularization; logistic loss appears in the finite-regularization experiments.

rows.subject: Generalized linear classifiers on raw real datasets
rows.operation_detail: Trained on random labels without preprocessing and compared training-loss curves with Gaussian theory.

conditions.value: MNIST, fashion-MNIST, grayscale CIFAR-10, and tiny ImageNet

rows.measure: Training loss as a function of n/p
rows.baseline: Gaussian theory using each dataset's covariance
rows.value: Authors report overall good agreement with very small deviations from Gaussian predictions.
rows.uncertainty: Simulations averaged over 10 samples; error bars not visible at plot scale.
rows.locator: Appendix C, Figure 5 and accompanying text
rows.note: Aggregate description across datasets; the paper attributes the small deviations to greater heterogeneity among mode covariance matrices. Training loss only.
rows.check: Small deviations from Gaussian training-loss predictions concern universality, not incomplete generalization under any version. The reported datasets and qualitative finding are otherwise consistent with Figure 5 and its accompanying text.
